items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: What’s the other guy? John Complain and Sarah Palin!

ctx.x: Are you going to be coming through St. Louis on your book tour?
I wish I could, that’s the home of Sarah Palin! What’s the other guy? John Complain and Sarah Palin! (Laughs) There’s the list! END OF INTERVIEW ### Transcribed by Kyle Kelly-Yahner

items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: I knew when Trane could play ballads and touch people you know.

ctx.x: — but it was created by African-Americans. And there were a few whites, even at that time, you know, Bix Beiderbecke and people back there, they were in that same mode. But the majority of the performers were African-Americans. Now all over the world there are people — you know I’ve been all over and I hear people playing like Sonny Rollins or Coltrane or Dizzy or whoever, from here, coming from all over the world. They’ve heard that music and they’ve absorbed some of the improvisational language.
Do you consider yourself — you grew up in the bebop era.

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He had played with ‘Trane, Sonny Rollins, Benny Golson, [Art] Farm[er]; he had played with everybody.

ctx.x: And how did you structure it?

Well, it is a compilation of all the giants who are still here, and some who are gone, their words endorsing me in a lot of cases, or speaking of experiences we had together. In doing so, I was very fortunate to have a few words from John Coltrane, from Dizzy. Those who are past on [such as] Art Farmer, and others, that I’ve come into contact with, and performed with, and had good times or bad times with.
Well, it’s a lot of time to cover so I imagine, you know, [it was] no small task. Is it something you’ve worked on sporadically over the years or have you been diligently putting it together?
